title: Mashup madness
content_html:
What We're Doing

In this activity, students act as "AI directors," combining the outputs of several different AI tools into one finished creative product — a technique often called a mashup pipeline. Instead of using a single AI tool in isolation, students will chain tools together: a chatbot writes a story or brand idea, an image generator turns that idea into a visual, a text-to-speech tool gives it a voice, and a design tool stitches everything into a single polished poster, comic, or mini-campaign.

The goal is to help students understand that AI tools have different specialities (text, image, sound, layout) and that real creative and commercial work often involves deliberately combining several tools — the same way a film crew has a scriptwriter, an artist, a voice actor, and an editor. Students will also see, first-hand, how the quality of what comes out of one tool depends heavily on the quality of the prompt that came from the tool (or human) before it.

By the end of the session, each student or pair will have produced one complete "AI Mashup" artefact — for example, a campaign poster for a made-up product, a story page with matching illustration and narration, or a mini "brand" for an invented character — built entirely by chaining AI tools together.

Tools & Resources

  • Chatbot (text generation): ChatGPT free tier — https://chat.openai.com (requires an account; free tier may rate-limit or queue during busy periods). Alternative: Microsoft Copilot — https://copilot.microsoft.com.
  • Image generator: Bing Image Creator — https://www.bing.com/images/create (free with a Microsoft account, but limited daily "boost" credits for fast generation — after that, images generate more slowly).
  • Backup / no-login image generator: Craiyon — https://www.craiyon.com (completely free, no account needed, but slower and lower-resolution — good for low-bandwidth situations or when accounts aren't available).
  • Text-to-speech tool: TTSMaker — https://ttsmaker.com (free, no login required, limited voice styles on the free tier).
  • Assembly / design tool: Canva — https://www.canva.com (free tier covers everything needed here; some premium templates and elements are locked). Alternative: Google Slides, which is fully free and works well for combining text, images, and audio links.
  • Optional backup device plan: Since this activity uses 3–4 tools, have a shared class device or two ready in case a student's tool is slow, blocked, or the free-tier limit is reached.

Step-by-Step Activity

  1. Warm-up (10 min): Explain the idea of an "AI mashup pipeline" using a simple diagram: Idea → Text AI → Image AI → Audio AI → Assembled Final Product. Show one finished example mashup (see Example Outputs below) before students start.
  2. Choose a brief (5 min): In pairs or individually, students pick (or are assigned) a creative brief. Suggested briefs: "Design a mascot and poster for a Nairobi recycling campaign," "Invent a new snack brand," or "Create a page from a picture book about a magical animal." Write the chosen brief at the top of a worksheet or document.
  3. Generate the core idea with a chatbot (15 min): Students open ChatGPT (or Copilot) and enter a prompt such as: "I'm designing a mascot and short slogan for a [recycling campaign / snack brand / picture book]. Give me: 1) a character name and short personality description, 2) a one-sentence slogan, 3) a vivid visual description of the character I could use to generate an image." Students should ask at least one follow-up question to refine the idea (e.g., "Make the character friendlier and add bright colours").
  4. Turn the text into an image prompt (10 min): Students copy the "visual description" from step 3 into the image generator (Bing Image Creator or Craiyon), adding style words such as "flat illustration style, bright colours, for children." Example prompt: "A friendly cartoon robot made of recycled bottles, big round eyes, holding a Kenyan flag-coloured recycling bin, flat illustration style, bright colours, white background."
  5. Generate and select an image (10 min): Students generate 2–3 image variations, compare them, and choose the best one — or edit their prompt to fix problems (e.g., "remove the extra arm," "make the background plain white").
  6. Create a voice or jingle line (10 min): Back in the chatbot, students ask: "Write a short, catchy 10-second jingle or spoken line that this character would say to encourage people to recycle." They paste this line into TTSMaker, choose a voice, and generate/download the audio clip.
  7. Assemble the mashup (20 min): Students open Canva or Google Slides and build a single poster/slide combining: the character image, the slogan, the jingle text (and audio file link, if the platform allows embedding), and the brief title. Encourage neat layout — image on one side, text on the other.
  8. Present (10 min): Each pair presents their mashup to the class in under a minute, explaining which tool did what and one thing they had to fix or re-prompt along the way.

Example Outputs

  • "Bao the Bottle Robot": A recycling campaign mascot — chatbot invented the name, personality, and slogan ("Bao says: don't waste it, recycle it!"), Bing Image Creator produced a friendly cartoon robot made of bottles, TTSMaker generated a cheerful jingle voice, and everything was combined into a one-page Canva poster with the slogan in bold at the top.
  • "Mango Blast" snack brand: Students invented a fictional fruit snack. The chatbot wrote a punchy tagline ("Mango Blast — sunshine in every bite!") and packaging description; the image tool generated a snack packet design; the final Canva slide showed a mock advertisement with the packet image, tagline, and a short voiced advert script.
  • Picture book page — "Nia and the Cloud Whale": The chatbot wrote a two-sentence story beat and a description of a whale made of clouds; the image tool generated the illustration; TTSMaker narrated the two sentences as if reading the page aloud; the final product was a single slide styled like a storybook page, ready to "read" aloud with the audio.

Facilitation Tips

  • Pacing: This activity moves through four tools in 90 minutes, so keep a visible countdown timer for each step and give a two-minute warning before each transition.
  • Free-tier limits: Warn students in advance that image credits and chatbot messages may run out. Encourage them to write good prompts the first time rather than generating many low-effort variations.
  • Odd or broken AI outputs: Image generators occasionally produce distorted faces, extra limbs, or garbled text. Treat this as a teaching moment about current AI limitations rather than a failure — ask "what do you think went wrong here?"
  • Prompt drift: Some students will describe their character differently in the image prompt than the chatbot originally suggested. Point this out as an example of how information can change (or get lost) as it passes between tools — just like in a real production pipeline.
  • Grouping: Pair a stronger reader/writer with a student who enjoys visual design so each step has an engaged owner.
  • Device/connectivity issues: Keep Craiyon as a fallback if Bing Image Creator is slow, blocked, or a Microsoft account isn't available.
  • Content control: Remind students that image and text generators will refuse or filter certain requests (violence, real people, etc.) — this is expected behaviour, not a bug.

Discussion Questions

  1. What is an "AI pipeline," and why might chaining several AI tools together create something a single tool couldn't make alone?
  2. Which tool in your pipeline struggled most to follow your instructions? Why do you think that happened?
  3. How much of the final mashup would you say was "created by you" versus "created by the AI"? Explain your thinking.
  4. Give one example of how changing the wording of a prompt changed what the next tool produced.
  5. Can you think of real jobs or products (adverts, games, apps, music videos) where teams likely combine multiple AI tools the way we did today?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Add a second character to your mashup that interacts with the first one (e.g., a friend, rival, or customer), generating a new image and short dialogue line for them.
  • Medium: Turn your mashup into a 3-panel comic strip. Use the chatbot to write three short story beats, generate a consistent-style image for each panel (try to keep the same character description across all three prompts), and add speech bubbles or captions.
  • Hard: Build a full mini-campaign: text (slogan + short script), image (poster), audio (voiced advert), and a simple animation or slideshow transition (using Canva's animate feature or a similar free tool). Present it as a 60-second "pitch" to the class, explaining the role each AI tool played and one ethical consideration (e.g., could this mascot mislead people, or whose voice/style was it trained on?).
